title: Urging Team Members to Play More Aggressively
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post argues that when a team has grown lethargic or complacent, the leader's request for more aggression and risk-taking is far easier to make early than late. Shifting a group from one mode of engagement to another takes time, and teams rarely have the reserves to jump from zero to sixty. The author draws an analogy to strict discipline: it is easier to lighten up over time than to turn the dial up. The move is a timing rule: set the intensity expectation at the start of a season, project or sales cycle, then regulate it as needed. He closes on the claim that risk-taking comes more easily to teams that have already taken some.
points: Asking a team for more aggression is a timing problem: the request lands best before a rhythm or style of play sets.
Intensity is asymmetric, since a leader can always dial a team back but struggles to raise urgency from a relaxed climate.
Shifting people from one engagement style to another takes time, so leaders cannot expect an instant change of gear.
Early risk-taking builds the habit that makes later risk-taking possible.
quotes: Asking team members to find another gear and to ratchet up their aggressiveness isn’t as easy as it sounds. It takes time for people to shift from one mode or style of engagement to another, especially when the request is to take more risks and chances.
The better leadership choice is to make this request early in the project, sales cycle, game, or initiative before the rhythm or style of play gets set.

Similar to leading with strict discipline or rules, it is easier to lighten up over time than it is to turn up the dial. Preaching aggressiveness early in a year, a season, or in a project allows leaders to regulate intensity as they see fit. The team can always dial it back later on, but it is much harder to increase the intensity and urgency after starting from a relaxed climate.
But going from zero to 60 in three seconds takes a tremendous amount of horsepower, and most teams lack the ability to find those energy reserves.
The best leaders know that taking risks is easier when the team has already taken some.
